cards.statement: Counting TLS alone, a basic full TLS 1.3 handshake lets clients send data after one round trip.
cards.explanation: TLS 1.3 clients send 1-RTT data after Finished.

source.title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3

cards.statement: A TLS 1.3 client answers HelloRetryRequest within the original handshake round trip.
cards.explanation: HelloRetryRequest adds a round trip for another ClientHello.

source.title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3

cards.statement: A TLS 1.3 server gains cross-connection replay protection from 0-RTT record encryption.
cards.explanation: TLS 1.3 gives early data no cross-connection replay guarantee.

source.title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3

cards.statement: A TLS 1.3 server encrypts its certificate during the handshake.
cards.explanation: TLS 1.3 encrypts Certificate with handshake keys.

source.title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3

cards.statement: TLS 1.3 public-key exchanges provide forward secrecy for 1-RTT application traffic.
cards.explanation: Long-term-key compromise does not reveal previous traffic keys.

source.title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3

cards.statement: A TLS 1.3 endpoint negotiates a separate MAC algorithm for record protection.
cards.explanation: TLS 1.3 protects records with AEAD.
cards.misconception: Record protection negotiates a separate MAC.

source.title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3

cards.statement: A TLS 1.3 client sends ClientHello to renegotiate an established connection.
cards.explanation: TLS 1.3 forbids renegotiation on established connections.

source.title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3

cards.statement: A TLS 1.3 server chooses the version from ClientHello's legacy_version field.
cards.explanation: TLS 1.3 negotiates versions through supported_versions.

source.title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3

cards.statement: A TLS 1.3 sender places its own certificate first in the transmitted chain.
cards.explanation: The first certificate identifies the peer being authenticated.

source.title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3

cards.statement: A TLS client can put a server's literal IP address in the SNI host_name field.
cards.explanation: SNI host_name carries a DNS hostname; literal IP addresses are forbidden.

source.title: Transport Layer Security (TLS) Extensions: Extension Definitions

cards.statement: A TLS client accepting wildcards matches * in *.example.net against exactly one DNS label.
cards.explanation: A TLS wildcard for *.example.net covers api.example.net, rather than a.b.example.net.

source.title: Service Identity in TLS

cards.statement: A TLS client using ECH sends an encrypted ClientHelloInner inside a public ClientHelloOuter.
cards.explanation: The inner message holds private parameters; the outer message carries their ciphertext.
cards.volatilityNote: ECH is a newly specified extension whose protocol guidance may evolve.

source.title: TLS Encrypted Client Hello

cards.statement: A QUIC sender carries TLS handshake bytes in CRYPTO frames instead of TLS records.
cards.explanation: QUIC supplies its own framing and packet protection for TLS handshake bytes.

source.title: Using TLS to Secure QUIC

cards.statement: A QUIC receiver uses a packet's nonempty Destination Connection ID to find its connection.
cards.explanation: Connection IDs associate arriving packets with connection state.

source.title: QUIC: A UDP-Based Multiplexed and Secure Transport

cards.statement: A QUIC server sends application data on a unidirectional stream opened by its client.
cards.explanation: The client sends data on its client-initiated unidirectional stream.

source.title: QUIC: A UDP-Based Multiplexed and Secure Transport

cards.statement: A QUIC receiver uses STREAM offsets to reconstruct the byte order within an individual stream.
cards.explanation: Offsets identify where received data belongs in the stream.

source.title: QUIC: A UDP-Based Multiplexed and Secure Transport

cards.statement: A QUIC receiver raises a stream's individual data limit by increasing its connection-level limit.
cards.explanation: QUIC tracks stream and connection limits separately; raising connection credit leaves the stream limit unchanged.
cards.misconception: Connection credit also increases the individual stream limit.

source.title: QUIC: A UDP-Based Multiplexed and Secure Transport

cards.statement: A QUIC sender can retransmit lost stream data using the original packet number.
cards.explanation: QUIC resends stream data in a newly numbered packet, making individual transmission acknowledgments unambiguous.
cards.misconception: Stream retransmission reuses its original packet number.

source.title: QUIC Loss Detection and Congestion Control

cards.statement: A QUIC endpoint tracks Initial, Handshake and application data in separate packet number spaces.
cards.explanation: QUIC separates packet acknowledgments across these spaces; 0-RTT and 1-RTT share the application-data space.

source.title: Using TLS to Secure QUIC

cards.statement: A QUIC sender can choose CUBIC in place of the NewReno-like congestion controller.
cards.explanation: QUIC's congestion signals accommodate alternative sender-side algorithms; its specified controller is an example.

source.title: QUIC Loss Detection and Congestion Control

cards.statement: A QUIC server bases its pre-validation amplification budget on the number of received packets.
cards.explanation: Before validation, a server limits outgoing bytes to three times received bytes.

source.title: QUIC: A UDP-Based Multiplexed and Secure Transport

cards.statement: A QUIC client must make the UDP payload carrying an Initial packet at least 1200 bytes long.
cards.explanation: The client pads or coalesces packets to meet this minimum.

source.title: QUIC: A UDP-Based Multiplexed and Secure Transport

cards.statement: A QUIC server's Version Negotiation packet selects the version for the client's next connection attempt.
cards.explanation: The packet lists offered versions. The client selects a mutually supported version for its new first flight.
cards.misconception: The server's packet chooses the retry version.

source.title: Compatible Version Negotiation for QUIC

cards.statement: A QUIC sender automatically resends DATAGRAM frames when their packets are declared lost.
cards.explanation: QUIC's DATAGRAM extension leaves lost datagrams unretransmitted, even though their packets elicit acknowledgments.
cards.misconception: The QUIC transport retransmits lost DATAGRAM frames.

source.title: An Unreliable Datagram Extension to QUIC
